content: Angioedema is a condition characterized by swelling that occurs beneath the skin, unlike hives, which are surface swellings often referred to as welts. It is possible to experience angioedema without the presence of hives. The primary symptom of angioedema is sudden swelling beneath the skin's surface. This swelling often occurs around the eyes and lips but can also affect the hands, feet, and throat. The swelling may appear as a localized line or spread out more diffusely. Welts, if present, are typically painful and may itch. They can become pale and swell further if irritated. The deeper swelling associated with angioedema can also be painful. Additional symptoms may include abdominal cramping, difficulty breathing, swollen eyes and mouth, and swelling of the lining of the eyes (chemosis). Angioedema can be triggered by an allergic reaction, during which histamine and other chemicals are released into the bloodstream. This release occurs when the immune system identifies a foreign substance, known as an allergen. However, in many cases, the exact cause of angioedema remains unknown. Potential triggers include animal dander, exposure to water, sunlight, cold, or heat, certain foods (such as berries, shellfish, fish, nuts, eggs, and milk), insect bites, medications (such as antibiotics like penicillin and sulfa drugs, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors), and pollen. Angioedema and hives may also develop following infections or in association with other illnesses, including autoimmune disorders like lupus, as well as leukemia and lymphoma. A hereditary form of angioedema exists, which has distinct triggers, complications, and treatments, but it is not covered in this discussion. To diagnose angioedema, a physician will examine the skin and inquire about exposure to potential irritants. If the throat is affected, a physical exam may reveal abnormal breathing sounds, such as stridor. In rare cases, blood tests or allergy testing may be performed. It is crucial to seek medical attention if angioedema does not respond to treatment, is severe, or occurs for the first time. Emergency care should be sought immediately if symptoms include abnormal breathing sounds (stridor), difficulty breathing, fainting, or wheezing. Treatment for angioedema depends on the severity of symptoms. Mild cases may not require treatment, while moderate to severe cases often do. Breathing difficulties constitute a medical emergency. Cool compresses or soaks can help alleviate pain. Medications commonly used to treat angioedema include antihistamines, corticosteroids (anti-inflammatory drugs), epinephrine, ranitidine (Zantac), and terbutaline (a bronchodilator). In severe cases where breathing is compromised, a tube may be inserted into the throat to maintain an open airway. Patients diagnosed with angioedema should avoid certain medications, including benazepril, captopril, quinapril, ramipril, trandolapril, enalapril maleate, and lisinopril. It is essential to consult a physician before starting or discontinuing any of these medications. Angioedema that does not affect breathing is generally harmless and resolves within a few days, although it can be uncomfortable. However, complications such as anaphylactic reactions or life-threatening airway obstruction (if swelling occurs in the throat) can arise. To prevent angioedema from recurring, avoid irritating the affected area and steer clear of known allergens. Never take medications that are not prescribed for you.
